content: The heterophile antibody test, also known as the mononuclear spot test or monospot test, is a rapid diagnostic tool used to detect infectious mononucleosis caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). This test is an advancement over the older Paul-Bunnell test. It specifically identifies heterophile antibodies produced by the human immune system in response to an EBV infection. Commercially available test kits have a sensitivity ranging from 70% to 92% and a specificity between 96% and 100%. However, the sensitivity is lower during the first two weeks after the onset of clinical symptoms. The test is generally not positive during the 4-6 week incubation period before symptoms appear, nor is it typically positive after the active infection has resolved, even though the virus remains latent in the host's cells for life. The test works by detecting the agglutination of horse red blood cells (RBCs) caused by heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum. The term heterophile refers to antibodies that react with proteins across species lines or with antigens other than the one that originally stimulated their production (cross-reactive antibodies). A 20% suspension of horse RBCs is prepared in an isotonic solution containing 3-8% sodium citrate. To perform the test, one drop of the patient’s serum is mixed on an opal glass slide with one drop of a particulate suspension of guinea pig kidney stroma and a suspension of beef red cell stroma. The mixtures are stirred with a wooden applicator 10 times. Then, 10 microliters of the horse RBC suspension are added to each drop of adsorbed serum and mixed. The mixture is left undisturbed for one minute without rocking or shaking. The presence or absence of red cell agglutination is then observed. If agglutination is stronger with the serum adsorbed with guinea pig kidney stroma, the test is positive. If agglutination is stronger with the serum adsorbed with beef red cell stroma, the test is negative. If no agglutination occurs in either mixture, the test is negative. Positive and negative control sera are tested alongside each batch of patient samples to ensure accuracy. The test is indicated as a confirmatory diagnostic tool when a physician suspects EBV infection, particularly in the presence of clinical features such as fever, malaise, pharyngitis, tender lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical lymph nodes, often referred to as tender glands), and splenomegaly. The test has a very high specificity, nearly 100%, making a positive result highly reliable for confirming EBV infection. However, false-positive results can occasionally occur in conditions such as toxoplasmosis, rubella, lymphoma, and leukemia. The sensitivity of the test is moderate, meaning a negative result does not rule out EBV infection. This limitation is especially pronounced in young children, many of whom do not produce heterophile antibodies at any stage of the infection, leading to false-negative results. In cases of delayed or absent seroconversion, an immunofluorescence test may be employed if the diagnosis remains uncertain.
